<strong>Confusión</strong> (S-boxes no l: Confusion (non-linear S-boxes) and diffusion (permutations and mixings), on a small scale and in many rounds: the substitution-permutation network.
<strong>Confusión</strong>: que la relac: Confusion: that the relation between the key and the ciphertext be as tangled as possible, none of the linear equations that are solved as in Hill. It is achieved with substitution boxes, small non-linear tables.
<strong>Difusión</strong>: que cada bit: Diffusion: that each bit of the message influence many bits of the ciphertext, so that the frequencies and any other regularity are spread out and disappear. It is achieved with bit permutations and mixings.
<strong>La permutación.</strong> Bits en: The permutation. Bits at positions 0 to 7: $1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0$. Bit 0 goes to position 0; bit 3 goes to $2\cdot 3 + 0 = 6$. The rest are zeros. Result: $1000\,0010$.
<strong>Lo que se ve.</strong> El uno de: What can be seen. The one at position 3, which came out of the first S-box, has ended up in the second half: in the next round it will go into the other S-box. That is diffusion: what the S-box changes is spread over the whole block.
Al revés: que cambie poco significa que: The other way round: changing little means the ciphertext preserves the message's structure. Security lies in half of it changing, and at random.

Claude Shannon definió confusión y difus: Claude Shannon defined confusion and diffusion in his 1949 paper. Horst Feistel designed at IBM, around 1971, the first modern block cipher, Lucifer, from which DES came in 1977. Eli Biham and Adi Shamir published differential cryptanalysis in 1990, and it became known then that the IBM team and the NSA had known of it since the seventies and had designed DES's S-boxes to resist it, in secret. Mitsuru Matsui published the linear one in 1993. With those two tools the AES candidates were evaluated in 1998, and the winner, Rijndael, was designed by proving that neither technique got beyond four rounds.

Con una ronda, el cifrado es una S-box y: With one round, the cipher is an S-box and a permutation, and Eve writes down the table. With two, she can still approximate the S-box by a linear equation that is right, say, 75 % of the time, and that approximation propagates. But on chaining rounds the approximations multiply: if each is right with probability $1/2 + \varepsilon$, the $r$ together give a bias of the order of $\varepsilon^r$, which sinks exponentially. It is the idea of linear and differential cryptanalysis, and also the reason AES has ten rounds and not two: it was calculated how many were needed for no approximation to survive, and a few more were added as margin.

Un bloque de 16 bits, una clave de 16 bi: A 16-bit block, a 16-bit key and up to four rounds. In each round: XOR with the round key, S-box on each group of 4 bits and permutation of the 16 bits (except in the last one, where it adds nothing). Change one bit of the block or of the key and look at how many change at the output.
Un bloque de 8 bits, 1011 0010, con clav: An 8-bit block, 1011 0010, with round key 0110 1100. Apply XOR with the key, the table's S-box to each group of 4 bits, and then the permutation that crosses the bits: bit $i$ goes to position $2(i \bmod 4) + \lfloor i/4 \rfloor$ (numbering from 0 to 7 from the left).
Un cifrado por bloques de 64 bits cambia: A 64-bit block cipher changes, on average, 12 output bits when one input bit is changed. What does that indicate?
Un cifrado por bloques es la pieza con l: A block cipher is the piece with which almost everything else is built: with it whole hard disks are encrypted, every packet of a secure connection is protected, random number generators and hash functions are manufactured. AES, the one you will see in two topics, has been built into processors as an instruction since 2010, and that is why encrypting a whole disk is not noticeable when using the computer. And linear and differential cryptanalysis, born to attack these networks, are today the test every new cipher has to pass before being published.
Un cifrado por bloques es una permutació: A block cipher is a permutation of the $2^n$ blocks chosen by the key, computed with a short recipe.
Un cifrado por bloques toma un trozo de: A block cipher takes a piece of message of fixed size, today 128 bits, and turns it into another of the same size with a key. It is a gigantic permutation of the $2^{128}$ possible blocks, chosen by the key. Nobody can write that table down; what is written is a short recipe that computes it, and the recipe was given by Shannon in 1949 in two words: confusion and diffusion.
Una S-box con fórmula, pocas rondas o un: An S-box with a formula, too few rounds or a permutation at the end are the classic mistakes.
Una permutación al final es pública y no: A permutation at the end is public and mixes nothing further: Eve undoes it for free. That is why the last round carries only S-box and key.
